In this series of posts, we’ll be featuring mathematical video and streaming channels from all over the internet, by speaking to the creators of the channel and asking them about what they do.

We spoke to Ellie Sleightholm about her YouTube channel, on which she posts roughly once a week to share the beauty in mathematics.

Channel title: Ellie Sleightholm
Link: youtube.com/elliesleightholm (YouTube) or instagram.com/ellieinstem (Instagram)
Topics covered: Mainly mathematics but also cover videos on space and technology
Average video length: 15 minutes on YouTube; 60 seconds on Instagram
Recommended videos: Derivatives Aren’t What You Think They Are, Mathematician Visits Artemis II – Here’s What I Learned, and The Mathematics in Machine Learning 

What is your channel about, and why did it start?

My channel is about uncovering the beauty of mathematics! Mathematics is everywhere, even in places you’d least expect, and through my channel I aim to showcase that. A lot of people might have negative experiences with maths at school and I want to show them that it is so much deeper and more beautiful than how you may have been taught at school. I’m basically one big maths nerd and I love sharing that with the world! My channel started when I was studying mathematics at university. It was initially to film day in the life content and after I graduated, I transitioned into making more fun, educational style content. 

Who are you? Tell us about yourself.

My name is Ellie Sleightholm. I’m a Mathematics Graduate with a BSc from the University of Leeds and a MASt (Masters) in Part III Mathematics at the University of Cambridge. After my degree, I worked in the space industry for 2 years as a Space Systems Optimisation Engineer and then an Astrodynamics Software Engineer. I got to incorporate my love for mathematics and coding in these roles. I then worked in the AI/Machine Learning industry for 2 years developing innovative technologies and also creating educational content which I loved too! I am currently working for Veritasium, the science YouTube channel, and will be pursuing a PhD in Applied Mathematics at the University of Cambridge in October 2026.

Who is the intended audience for your channel? 

Anyone who wants to appreciate the beauty of mathematics! I try to make all my content accessible so people above GCSE level can engage and learn something from it. 

What is a typical video like? 

A typical video usually includes a specific topic that I discuss the mathematics around. So for example, I picked Machine Learning for my latest video and explained some mathematics used there. For my non-mathematics videos, these are more documentary style in format including interviews with experts. An example of this is my video of my visit to Germany for Artemis II. 

Why should people watch your videos?

If you love watching other people nerd out about mathematics then my content is for you :) I’m a firm believer that while we can claim ‘mathematics is everywhere’, people don’t really understand how much so until they are exposed to it. That’s the aim of my channel. I want you to go and make your morning cup of coffee, look at the mixing and remember a video from my channel talking about the mathematics in that cup. Or if you’re on your daily walk and you stop by a Fern bush, I want you to remember the video I did on the transformations involved in making such a beautiful piece of nature. If you want to connect with the world around you from a mathematical perspective, that’s what I aim to do on my channel! 

What are some highlights of the channel so far?

I’ve genuinely enjoyed making every piece of content on my channel but I have really loved making more documentary/real-world explainer content. I was fortunate enough to be invited by NASA to watch the launch of Artemis II in Florida as well as invited to Germany to see firsthand Europe’s involvement in the mission. I loved being able to speak to the people involved in the mission and share that with my audience.

The full videos are here: 
NASA Invites Mathematician to Watch the Launch of Artemis II
Mathematician Visits Artemis II… Here’s What I Learned

For my more mathematical content, I love looking at things around me and finding the hidden, beautiful mathematical structures. I did a video on the mathematics behind the Barnsley Fern which I loved putting together.

What exciting plans do you have for the future? 

Much more content! I’ve really enjoyed doing both mathematical deep dives as well as documentary style content so both of those will continue to be released on my channel. I’m also excited about filming on location with other mathematicians! Of course, as I embark on my PhD journey, I’d also love to share a glimpse into what I get up to and the mathematics that I learn there too.

Here’s a short round-up of maths news from this month.

The 2026 Fields medals have been awarded to Yu Deng, John Pardon, Jacob Tsimerman and Hong Wang. The Fields Medal is awarded to recognize outstanding mathematical achievement for existing work and for the promise of future achievement, and this year’s winners work across PDEs, symplectic geometry, algebraic geometry, harmonic analysis and measure theory.

Hannah Fry has been awarded the IMU’s Leelavati prize for increasing public awareness of maths. “She has become a voice for mathematics that resonates far beyond the public audience normally interested in science communication. Through a wide range of media – including books, videos, and television programs – she has used outstanding creativity and originality to translate mathematics into a language of wonder and relevance for the public without diminishing its scope and importance.”

A result in braid theory has been proven by a team including Joan Birman, aged 99. The proof “reveals brand new insights into the geometry of braids” and closes the \(n=4\) case of the long-standing question of whether the Burau representation of the braid group is faithful. (via @gregegansf@mathstodon.xyz)

The theme selected for the 2027 International Day of Mathematics is ‘Mathematics, AI and Our Future’. “The theme explores the role of mathematics as the foundation of artificial intelligence and how mathematical ideas shape one of today’s most transformative technologies.”

In this series of posts, we’ll be featuring mathematical video and streaming channels from all over the internet, by speaking to the creators of the channel and asking them about what they do.

We spoke to Kala, who has an Instagram channel called MathsWithKala.

Channel title: @MathsWithKala
Link: instagram.com/mathswithkala/
Topics covered: Mathematics around us, unexpected uses of pure mathematics research, debunking stereotypes about mathematicians, life of a female British-Hungarian postdoc in pure maths 
Average video length: 1 minute
Recommended videos: Maths powers your phone, Girl math is just math, Being pretty and being good at maths are unrelated, POV: you’re sitting in the audience and suddenly your theorem is on the board

What is your channel about, and when/why did it start?

MathsWithKala is all about showing that mathematics is everywhere, sharing unexpected uses of pure mathematics, challenging stereotypes about mathematicians, and giving people a glimpse into my life as a British-Hungarian postdoctoral researcher in pure mathematics.

The idea for the channel first came to me when I was an undergraduate at the University of St Andrews. A friend wrote an article for the student newspaper about women in mathematics and suggested that I should start sharing my experiences online to make female mathematicians more visible. I loved the idea, but it took me a while to build up the confidence. I eventually started posting consistently in December 2025.

Who are you?

I’m Kala, also known as Dr Kamilla Rekvényi, and I’m currently a Research Fellow at the University of Manchester.

I grew up in Hungary and always loved mathematics, but the stereotypes surrounding mathematicians affected me growing up. I competed in lots of maths competitions in secondary school and noticed that I often didn’t fit the stereotype of what people expected a mathematician to be. I decided that if I was going to stand out, I was going to really stand out, so I embraced my love of pink and my feminine style instead of hiding it.

I moved to the UK to study mathematics at the University of St Andrews, where I realised I wanted to become an academic mathematician. After completing my PhD at Imperial College London, I joined the University of Manchester as a Research Fellow.

Today, my goal is to be the visible mathematician that I wished I’d had growing up – someone young people, especially girls, can relate to.

Who is the intended audience for the channel?

Anyone who loves mathematics, or anyone who doesn’t know yet that they could!

I’d love to inspire more young girls to see that there are people like them in mathematics. If even a handful of girls feel more confident about pursuing maths because of my videos, I’ll consider that a success.

I also want to reach people who think they “just aren’t maths people” and show them that mathematics is creative, beautiful and surprisingly accessible. One of my favourite moments so far was when a friend from Pilates (I’m also training to become a Pilates instructor) told me she’d never imagined she could enjoy or understand higher-level maths, but one of my videos had made a concept click for her. That’s exactly the kind of impact I hope to have.

What is a typical video like?

I usually post two or three short reels each week. They typically include:

  • a lifestyle video about life as a mathematician;
  • content about women in mathematics and challenging stereotypes; and
  • an accessible explanation of a mathematical idea, a beautiful theorem, a useful mathematical tool, or a surprising real-world application of mathematics.

Most of my videos are around one minute long.

Why should people watch?

I don’t take myself too seriously. I want to show that maths is fun, fascinating and all around us, and that you don’t have to be a genius to enjoy it. I also want people to see that mathematicians are just ordinary people who happen to spend their days thinking about unusual questions.

I tend to focus on the big picture rather than technical details. Instead of diving into formal proofs, I like to explain why a mathematical result is exciting, surprising or beautiful, and often share the personal stories or unexpected facts that make it memorable to me. I hope that by showing the more human side of mathematics, I can make abstract ideas feel approachable and spark people’s curiosity.

Anything else to share?

My version of the shirt that appears in this video that says “I’m too pretty to not do maths” is available to buy on my Etsy shop!
